raw_text:
### Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, characterized by high rates of hospitalization and mortality [1]. For decades, standard pharmacological management relied heavily on suppressing the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) [2, 3]. A landmark therapeutic shift occurred with the introduction of the first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), sacubitril/valsartan [4]. The drug combines RAAS blockade with the enhancement of endogenous vasoactive peptide systems [4]. Sacubitril is a prodrug metabolized to LBQ657, which inhibits neprilysin—the enzyme responsible for degrading beneficial natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [5]. Simultaneously, valsartan blocks the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor [6]. This synergistic action promotes vasodilation, natriuresis, and diuresis, while actively counteracting cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and sympathetic overactivation [6].

#### Evidence in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction

The clinical efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF; left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] ≤40%) was established by the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [1]. In this double-blind trial, 8,442 patients were randomized to receive either sacubitril/valsartan (97/103 mg twice daily) or enalapril (10 mg twice daily) [1]. Sacubitril/valsartan demonstrated a highly significant 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, alongside a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality [1]. A post-hoc analysis of mode of death revealed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced both sudden cardiac death and death from worsening HF by 20% and 21%, respectively [7]. These benefits were robust across the age spectrum [8] and were consistently observed even in patients who required dose reductions due to tolerability issues [9]. Furthermore, sacubitril/valsartan significantly improved health-related quality of life compared to enalapril [10].

To evaluate the safety and efficacy of initiating sacubitril/valsartan in the acute setting, the PIONEER-HF trial randomized 881 hospitalized HFrEF patients stabilized after an acute decompensation episode [11]. In-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan led to a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) compared to enalapril, without an increase in adverse events such as worsening renal function or hyperkalemia [11]. The open-label extension of PIONEER-HF demonstrated that early initiation of sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a 42% reduction in the post-discharge composite endpoint of death, HF rehospitalization, or the need for a left ventricular assist device [12], showing similar benefits in Black Americans [13]. These findings were supported by the TRANSITION trial, which showed that starting sacubitril/valsartan either pre-discharge or early post-discharge was equally safe and feasible [14]. Additionally, the TITRATION trial outlined that both a condensed (3-week) and a conservative (6-week) up-titration regimen achieved high rates of target dose attainment with comparable tolerability [15].

#### Vascular Stiffness, Reverse Remodeling, and Cardiorenal Protection

The clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan are closely linked to left ventricular reverse remodeling. The PROVE-HF study demonstrated that initiating sacubitril/valsartan resulted in significant improvements in LVEF, left ventricular end-diastolic volume index, and left atrial volume index over 12 months, with cardiac remodeling closely correlating with the rapid reduction in NT-proBNP [16]. The EVALUATE-HF trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan improved left ventricular volumes and mitral remodeling, although it did not show a superior reduction in central aortic stiffness compared to enalapril over 12 weeks [17]. In the PRIME trial, sacubitril/valsartan proved superior to valsartan alone in reducing functional mitral regurgitation [18]. Functional improvements were also seen in the OUTSTEP-HF trial, which showed that switching to sacubitril/valsartan improved daily physical activity levels [19].

Beyond myocardial protection, sacubitril/valsartan provides important cardiorenal benefits. In a renal subanalysis of PARADIGM-HF, sacubitril/valsartan slowed the decline of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) compared to enalapril, especially in patients with type 2 diabetes [20], while also improving glycemic control [21]. The UK HARP-III trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan was safe and well-tolerated in patients with moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease [22]. Moreover, sacubitril/valsartan reduced the risk of severe hyperkalemia in patients concurrently taking mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [23].

#### Expansion Across the Spectrum of Ejection Fraction

Following its success in HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan was evaluated in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; LVEF ≥45%) in the PARAGON-HF trial [24], which built on the physiological improvements seen in the phase II PARAMOUNT trial [25]. In PARAGON-HF, sacubitril/valsartan compared to valsartan narrowly missed a statistically significant reduction in the primary endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death (hazard ratio 0.87, p=0.06) [24]. However, pre-specified subgroup analyses revealed a significant treatment benefit in patients with an LVEF below the median (45%–57%) and in women [24]. A prespecified pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF demonstrated that the benefits of sacubitril/valsartan extend to patients with an LVEF up to approximately 55%–60% [26].

For hospitalized patients with LVEF >40% and worsening HF, the PARAGLIDE-HF trial demonstrated that initiating sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP and was associated with a lower rate of renal events compared to valsartan [27]. A subsequent pooled participant-level analysis of PARAGON-HF and PARAGLIDE-HF confirmed a consistent reduction in cardiovascular and renal events across this patient population [28]. However, sacubitril/valsartan did not show clinical benefit in patients with advanced NYHA class IV HF in the LIFE trial [29] or in post-myocardial infarction patients without prior HF in the PARADISE-MI trial [30].

#### Guidelines and Clinical Recommendations

Based on this extensive evidence, the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines [2] and the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines [3] recommend sacubitril/valsartan as a Class I first-line or replacement therapy for HFrEF, and support its consideration in heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) and selected HFpEF patients on the lower LVEF spectrum.
